canonical_definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats safety as a latent model or agent property, disposition, or capability to avoid generating harmful, unsafe, toxic, offensive, unethical, illegal, or dangerous outputs, especially when facing malicious, adversarial, or otherwise unsafe prompts. Many definitions also tie this avoidance to alignment with human values, norms, or safety guidelines, and several make refusal central, describing safety as stopping models from following malicious instructions or producing benign responses to unsafe prompts. Smaller lines of work narrow the construct to security, meaning distinguishing malicious from normal inputs and refusing malicious questions, extend it to tool-using agents that should avoid harmful actions or environmental risks, or broaden it into a system-level trust-and-safety framing that includes protection from misinformation and abuse and user confidence.

Space of facets. Papers organize the construct through recurring facets: harmful or toxic content generation, refusal versus compliance on unsafe requests, jailbreak or adversarial resistance, and in some cases risky tool use or cross-lingual variation in refusal patterns. Some papers relabel the same general trait, for example as safety capability, while security alignment and LLM security use a narrower framing centered on detecting malicious inputs and keeping behavior within safe boundaries; a broader trust and safety framing adds user protection from misinformation, abuse, and unsafe content. Safety is also positioned alongside other alignment or evaluation dimensions rather than collapsed into them, and some work explicitly treats harmlessness as interchangeable with safety.

Space of measurement. Papers link safety to 30 measurement instruments and 9 behavioral indicators, with AdvBench, RewardBench, ToxiGen, TruthfulQA, and HarmBench appearing most often. The dominant operationalization is benchmark-based, using harmful instruction sets, refusal-versus-compliance tasks, toxicity or harmfulness classification, and adversarial or jailbreak evaluations; other papers use human pairwise judgments, LLM-as-a-judge comparisons, guard or moderation systems, and multimodal or spoken safety suites. In practice, this turns a latent disposition or capability into observable measures such as refusal rate, attack success rate, preference for refusal over compliance, toxicity scores, safe versus unsafe labels, or judgments of how benign a response is to unsafe prompts.

Links. Alignment is both claimed to have a causal relationship to safety and to be related to it. Safety is also related to harmlessness, sometimes interchangeably, and to helpfulness and robustness, and one paper places it within broader trustworthiness concerns. Additional single-paper claims describe causal relationships from intervention-style mechanisms to safety, and from safety to reduced helpfulness and over-rejection behavior; no correlational link is reported.

characterization_sections.text: Across papers, the prevailing usage treats safety as a latent model or agent property, disposition, or capability to avoid generating harmful, unsafe, toxic, offensive, unethical, illegal, or dangerous outputs, especially when facing malicious, adversarial, or otherwise unsafe prompts. Many definitions also tie this avoidance to alignment with human values, norms, or safety guidelines, and several make refusal central, describing safety as stopping models from following malicious instructions or producing benign responses to unsafe prompts. Smaller lines of work narrow the construct to security, meaning distinguishing malicious from normal inputs and refusing malicious questions, extend it to tool-using agents that should avoid harmful actions or environmental risks, or broaden it into a system-level trust-and-safety framing that includes protection from misinformation and abuse and user confidence.

characterization_sections.label: Space of facets.
characterization_sections.text: Papers organize the construct through recurring facets: harmful or toxic content generation, refusal versus compliance on unsafe requests, jailbreak or adversarial resistance, and in some cases risky tool use or cross-lingual variation in refusal patterns. Some papers relabel the same general trait, for example as safety capability, while security alignment and LLM security use a narrower framing centered on detecting malicious inputs and keeping behavior within safe boundaries; a broader trust and safety framing adds user protection from misinformation, abuse, and unsafe content. Safety is also positioned alongside other alignment or evaluation dimensions rather than collapsed into them, and some work explicitly treats harmlessness as interchangeable with safety.

characterization_sections.label: Space of measurement.
characterization_sections.text: Papers link safety to 30 measurement instruments and 9 behavioral indicators, with AdvBench, RewardBench, ToxiGen, TruthfulQA, and HarmBench appearing most often. The dominant operationalization is benchmark-based, using harmful instruction sets, refusal-versus-compliance tasks, toxicity or harmfulness classification, and adversarial or jailbreak evaluations; other papers use human pairwise judgments, LLM-as-a-judge comparisons, guard or moderation systems, and multimodal or spoken safety suites. In practice, this turns a latent disposition or capability into observable measures such as refusal rate, attack success rate, preference for refusal over compliance, toxicity scores, safe versus unsafe labels, or judgments of how benign a response is to unsafe prompts.

characterization_sections.label: Links.
characterization_sections.text: Alignment is both claimed to have a causal relationship to safety and to be related to it. Safety is also related to harmlessness, sometimes interchangeably, and to helpfulness and robustness, and one paper places it within broader trustworthiness concerns. Additional single-paper claims describe causal relationships from intervention-style mechanisms to safety, and from safety to reduced helpfulness and over-rejection behavior; no correlational link is reported.

definition_agreement.reason: Most papers define safety as a model's latent disposition or ability to avoid producing harmful, unsafe, toxic, offensive, or unethical outputs, often framed as refusing malicious or adversarial prompts and staying aligned with human or societal values. A few papers broaden this to tool-using agents, harmful actions, or general user protection, but these are minority extensions around the same central idea rather than a substantial competing definition.
